newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kiev reshuffle - out with the new, in with the old?.
newsitem.headline: Kiev reshuffle - out with the new, in with the old?.

text.p: Ukraine's new government, billed as an injection of fresh blood to push long-promised economic reforms, has a remarkably familiar look about it.

By simply recycling many current and former cabinet members, President Leonid Kuchma has failed to convince commentators and even some ministers that he has forged a team to accelerate reform in the face of growing scepticism from Western agencies and creditors.
"The term 'new government' raises a certain scepticism," Vyacheslav Pikhovshek, director of Kiev's Centre for Independent Political Research think-tank, said on Friday.

"You either believe the president when he says he has a limited selection of new blood to choose from, or else you believe some people were unjustly pushed out of the last government...It's rather a case of reshuffling an old deck of cards."

Kuchma has been trying to speed up economic reforms in the former Soviet republic of 51 million since launching them in late 1994. He began the round of hirings and firings last Friday following his nomination of new Prime Minister Valery Pustovoitenko on July 11.

Many ministers were simply re-appointed from the cabinet of Pavlo Lazarenko, who resigned a month ago. With the new cabinet almost complete, at least four others -- the agriculture, energy, statistics and coal ministers -- will returned to the government after a spell out of office.
Of those who departed, only former farm minister Mykhailo Zubets left the government altogether -- he is now of pensionable age.
Kuchma's top economic adviser defended the reshuffle, saying it had injected more experience into the cabinet line-up.

"Now the team consists not of those who are still learning to fly, but of experienced people," Anatoly Halchynsky told Reuters. "Over half the members of the last government had never worked in government before and had never even been to Kiev."

But even within the government, some are unsure how far the new team can speed up reforms. The doubts have been particularly expressed by Deputy Prime Minister Serhiy Tyhypko, a youthful banker appointed in April to oversee reform.
"We should wait before making conclusions. The appointments are one thing, but the real work is something different," Tyhypko said. "So far we cannot be satisfied with the work of the government."
The only fresh face among the economic portfolios is Economic Minister Viktor Suslov, who previously headed parliament's banking and finance committee.
Kuchma's advisers and Pustovoitenko described him as market-oriented economist but Suslov's former colleagues in parliament were not so sure.
"The appointment signals a move to the left in the government," said the leader of the nationalist Rukh party, Vyacheslav Chornovil. "Such a government won't be able to improve the situation."
The previous government, which struggled to push reforms through the conservative parliament, left an economy which shrank 7.5 percent in the first half after contracting by 10 percent last year.
The backlog of unpaid wages, pensions and student grants has swelled to 6.7 billion hryvnias ($3.6 billion).
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) recently decided not to grant a $2.7-$2.9 billion three-year credit to Ukraine, criticising Kiev for its failure to implement tax reforms.
For the time being the IMF is considering an interim standby loan but it will only be about $550 million -- less than the $750-$800 million which Kiev had expected.
The World Bank said on Thursday it had suspended a $317 million loan to Ukraine to develop its electricity market.

"I think that the West and people here especially are tired with constant presidential promises and declarations on reforms," reformist deputy Olexander Illyashkevych said. "This government will not be able to push reforms foward."
